text: Design a circular queue with a fixed capacity k. It needs six operations: enQueue, deQueue, Front, Rear, isEmpty, and isFull.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. There are six contracts, and the edge behaviour matters more than the algorithm here. enQueue and deQueue return a bool — false when the queue is full or empty, rather than throwing. And Front and Rear on an empty queue return negative one. Is that right?
Correct on all four.
Two more. What's the range on k — can it be zero? And what values can be stored? I'm asking because negative one is the sentinel, and I want to know whether it collides with a real value.
k is between one and one thousand, so never zero. Values are zero to one thousand, with up to three thousand calls.

Good — values are non-negative, so negative one is unambiguous, and k is at least one. I'll come back to k equals zero at the end, because there empty and full become the same thing. One thing worth flagging: zero is a legal value. So I can't use 'this slot holds zero' to mean the slot is unused — emptiness has to live entirely in the index bookkeeping.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would use a plain array and shift everything down after each dequeue — that's linear time per operation. This problem reminds me of the ring buffer pattern: keep a fixed array of size k and let the indices wrap with a single modulo capacity. The array stays linear; 'circular' lives entirely in the arithmetic. So the real design question is: which variables do I keep as state?
What are the options?

The obvious one is front and rear, and it's ambiguous. With k equals three, an empty queue has front and rear both at zero — and after three enqueues, they're both at zero again, but now it's full. Same two numbers, opposite states. Two standard fixes: waste a slot, or carry a boolean full flag. But both are repairs. The ambiguity comes from rear being a position, and positions wrap. What if I store size instead? Counts don't wrap. Empty is size equals zero, full is size equals capacity — opposite ends of a number line, never both true. And rear is still recoverable as front plus size minus one, mod capacity.
Are the other two wrong, then?

No — all three are correct. It's a design preference, not a correctness argument. The costs differ, though. Wasting a slot means array length and capacity are different numbers, so every modulo has to use k plus one, and using k by accident is an easy mistake. The flag costs no space but must be updated in two places — and a state you must remember to synchronize is a state you can forget to synchronize. Front and size cost nothing and need no upkeep. That's why I'd pick them.

Here's the plan. One: the first element is at front. Two: the next free slot is front plus size, mod capacity — skip the occupied slots. Three: the last element is one back from that, front plus size minus one, mod capacity. One thing worth flagging is that minus one — without it, Rear reads the next free slot, which holds a zero or a stale value, both plausible-looking. And deQueue doesn't touch the array at all: it just advances front and decrements size. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?
Sounds good. But you leave the old data sitting there? Doesn't that cause problems?

No, because membership is defined purely by the indices. A slot is in the queue exactly when its distance forward from front is less than size — the stored value never appears in that test. A stale value just gets overwritten when the indices wrap around. Clearing it would be worse: a pointless extra write, and writing zero to mean empty makes a real zero ambiguous. That's also why every operation is constant time in the worst case — no element is ever moved.

Alright, let me code this up. The state is front, size, and capacity, over a vector of exactly k slots. enQueue writes at front plus size, mod capacity, then bumps size. deQueue moves front forward by one, mod capacity, and decrements size. Front and Rear return negative one when empty. Two things worth pointing at. enQueue and deQueue call the public predicates, isFull and isEmpty, rather than re-implementing the check — so the guard and the reported state can never disagree. And every modulo sits behind a guard, which will matter in a second.
Trace it with k equals five through a wrap.

Let's dry-run the code. Enqueue ten, twenty, thirty, dequeue twice, then enqueue forty through seventy. Expected: front two, size five, and the array reads sixty, seventy, thirty, forty, fifty. The row that matters is enqueue sixty: front is two and size is three, so the slot is two plus three, mod five — zero. It wraps, and overwrites the stale ten from the first dequeue, without anyone ever having cleared it. Seventy lands in slot one, and the queue is full. That matches.
You called the Rear guard load-bearing. Why?

Because without it, an empty queue with front at zero computes negative one mod capacity. C++ truncates toward zero — the sign follows the dividend — so negative one mod five is negative one, not four. That's q of negative one, out of bounds. What makes it nasty is that it depends on k. At k equals one, negative one mod one is zero — in bounds. It doesn't crash or trip a sanitizer; it quietly returns a stale value from slot zero. So the same bug is invisible at k equals one, and an out-of-bounds read at k of two or more. Even with a safe modulo, I'd keep the guard — an empty queue owes the caller negative one.
How would you test this?

The input space is small enough to enumerate exhaustively. Six operations, and the state is two small integers. For k up to four, I can generate every operation sequence up to length seven and compare against a std deque reference. Two things I'd insist on. Compare the full queue contents after every single call, not just return values — a write-to-the-wrong-slot bug only surfaces several calls later. And assert every index is in bounds, because a bad index that lands in range, like the k equals one case, is silent otherwise. Then top it up with large k, and a long run that wraps front many times.

Let me think about complexity here. Every operation is constant time in the worst case, not amortized — there's no hash table, so no rehashing. Space is exactly k ints, with no pointers and nothing to leak. Overflow isn't reachable: front plus size peaks at nineteen ninety-nine. Oh, one more thing — at k equals zero, this code happens to be safe. isEmpty and isFull are both true, so every operation returns early and no modulo by zero is reached. Still, if the constraint were relaxed, I'd add an explicit capacity-zero guard, because relying on that is correct but fragile.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You dissolved the full-versus-empty ambiguity instead of patching it — positions wrap and counts don't. You were careful to say the other two approaches are correct, separating a correctness argument from a preference. And your testing answer was the strongest part: checking the contents after every call, and knowing why the k equals one case slips past a sanitizer. Good work.
